prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: I opened with IceCube (B012) first and the lattice clock third, and having read all eight ballots I now put the lattice clock first. Seven of eight members ranked it, six placed it in their top three, and nobody gave a substantive objection that survives scrutiny. The science is a measurement achievement of the kind I trust: Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the light-shift perturbation, and Ye's group and others then took neutral-atom clocks to about 1e-18 fractional uncertainty. Independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST, NPL) reproduce this and compare clocks across fibre links, so the confirmation question I always ask is answered. The credited contribution is decisive: a two-name prize, with the concept and first lattice clocks from Katori and the precision and many-body frontier from Ye, is as clean as attribution gets on this shortlist. The consequences are concrete (tests of constants and dark-matter couplings, centimetre-scale relativistic geodesy, the pending redefinition of the second) and the physics will last.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to earlier prizes. The 2005 prize (Hall, Haensch) gave us the frequency comb, and the 2012 prize (Wineland, Haroche) covered quantum control of ions, which also underpins the best ion clocks. A sceptic can say that lattice clocks are a very successful application of recognised tools, and that Al+ and Sr+ ion clocks compete for the same credit. The other risk is timing: the redefinition of the second has not happened yet, and one could wait for it. I think neither argument is decisive, because the lattice concept and its realisation are a distinct, original step and the performance is already established. Separately, if the committee wants a discovery about nature rather than an instrument, B012 is my stronger candidate and I would not want it lost.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first as a textbook case of a technique that moved the precision frontier by orders of magnitude, and notes that the 2005 and 2012 prizes might be seen as covering part of this ground.
responses.response: I agree with the measurement framing and with the reproduction record you list. On the prior-prize objection I side with you: the comb is the ruler and ion control is a different platform, whereas the magic-wavelength lattice with many atoms interrogated at once is a separate idea that delivers the stability advantage. I would add one point you did not raise: ion clocks (Al+, Sr+) reach comparable accuracy, so the citation should name the lattice technique specifically and not 'optical clocks' in general. I also disagree mildly with the idea of waiting for the SI second to be redefined; a prize should follow the demonstrated science, not a metrology-committee timetable.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first for its clean atomic physics (engineering the light shift), and says two laureates give a clear and fair configuration. She also flags a collaboration with Keller, bearing on B003.
responses.response: Your point about engineering the light shift is what convinces me that this is more than an application of the comb. I accept your attribution argument that other Sr and Yb groups refined but did not originate the idea. Your recusal disclosure on B003 is the right thing to do, and it reinforces my reluctance to build a configuration on the Ti:sapphire candidate, where the committee would also have to sort out the Kerr-lens history (Sibbett versus Spence). I would ask you to confirm whether you see any similar closeness to Katori or Ye, since you are the member best placed to say.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube first, with Halzen and Karle, and argues that it is a discovery found through clues from nature with lasting multimessenger impact, while ranking the lattice clock third.
responses.response: I share this view and ranked IceCube first myself, so this is a qualification of my own opening position and not a disagreement with yours. What moved me is the allocation problem we both flagged: with a thousand-person collaboration, AMANDA and DUMAND precursors, Yoshida in the credited set, and NGC 1068 at roughly four sigma, a defensible two- or three-name citation is much harder to write for IceCube than for the clock. Only two of us ranked B012 and no one else has argued for it, so I would like to hear whether Eriksson, Mehlig or Johansson see a scientific objection or simply less familiarity. I keep it as my first alternative and would support it in a later round if the clock stalls.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks fluctuation theorems first for being exact, general results with broad reach, and places the lattice clock fifth as possibly an incremental step after previous clock and comb prizes.
responses.response: I take your point that B032 has rigorous, experimentally confirmed content, and I defer to you on its physics since stochastic thermodynamics is outside my expertise. My concern is attribution, which you yourself describe as genuinely contested among Evans, Jarzynski, Crooks, Seifert and the Cohen-Morriss-Searles line, and which forces a cut that I think the committee would struggle to defend. On the incremental objection, I disagree: going from the 1e-15 regime to 1e-18 with a new trapping scheme is a qualitative change in what can be measured, not a refinement. If you can show the committee a clean three-name story for B032 I will read it with an open mind.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks DMFT first for its lasting conceptual and practical impact on correlated-electron theory, but identifies the omission of Metzner from the credited set as a real attribution risk.
responses.response: The Metzner omission is, in my view, a more serious problem than your ballot suggests: Vollhardt and Metzner introduced the infinite-dimensional limit, which is the foundation, and a prize that skips one of the two would be hard to justify. You also say that the accuracy of DFT+DMFT for specific materials is uneven. Since I cannot judge the theory itself, I ask for a fuller account of what the independent experimental tests of DMFT predictions actually are, beyond agreement with photoemission and optical data, before I could rank B018 near the top.

uncertainties: Priority between Katori and parallel proposals for magic-wavelength trapping (for example Lemonde, Derevianko, Pal'chikov) has not been verified from primary records in this process.
Whether the committee regards lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and whether ion-clock groups would have to be named.

Whether the individual-credit problem for B012 (Halzen, Karle, Yoshida, AMANDA and Baikal precursors) can be resolved into a clean citation, and whether Eriksson, Mehlig or Johansson have scientific objections to it.
AMO and metrology are outside my own expertise, so I rely on Lindroth, Kroll and Johansson for the physics detail of B007.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile for B007. I work in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations, none of which is involved in optical clocks. B012 (IceCube) is in my own broad field of astroparticle physics and I know that community professionally, so I flag that proximity for the committee's information, though my profile does not show any collaboration with the credited candidates.
